Below is a forward-looking roadmap for harnessing natural compounds to combat aluminum toxicity, organized around four priorities: comparative efficacy studies, nanotechnology-enabled delivery, integration with lifestyle interventions, and strategies to bridge from preclinical promise to clinical use.

1) Why natural compounds and what mechanisms matter
Aluminum exposure arises from diet, cookware, medicines, and water, with ionic Al accumulating in brain, liver, and bone and driving oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammatory cascades, and proteinopathy-like changes (e.g., Aβ/tau alterations), alongside organ dysfunction in liver and heart <cite id="968752ec-1">The metal is widely present in consumer products and the environment; ionic Al is measurable in tissues and fluids, and exposure elevates organ burdens with oxidative, apoptotic, and mitochondrial mechanisms</cite> <cite id="968752ec-2">Aluminum transported to brain, liver, and bones provokes ROS, inflammation, Aβ and tau pathology, cholinergic disruption, and hepatic enzyme elevations with lipid metabolism impairment</cite>. Natural products act through complementary mechanisms: metal-chelation or sequestration (notably flavonoids), direct radical scavenging and phase II enzyme induction (polyphenols, vitamins), mitochondrial and synaptic support (e.g., curcumin), and gut–brain–liver modulation (probiotics and dietary phenolics) <cite id="968752ec-0">Natural products can chelate or neutralize aluminum; curcumin shows BBB penetration after nanosizing and mitochondrial support; hesperidin and carnosine attenuate neuroinflammation/caspase activation; rosemary/oregano/resveratrol/quercetin/propolis/apigenin/royal jelly protect tissues; probiotic Lactobacillus plantarum CCFM639 lowered aluminum levels; generally safe with few side effects</cite> <cite id="5585b703-1">Flavonoids and other natural antioxidants increase methylation capacity and ROS scavenging, induce phase II detoxification and CYP enzymes, and exhibit chelation for metals, with examples like naringenin normalizing hepatic/renal functions in toxicant models</cite> <cite id="5585b703-0">Flavonoids/polyphenols in Tamarindus indica fractions likely combat oxidative stress in aluminum-exposed fetal rat brain via chelation and antioxidant signaling, improving sensory-motor and histologic outcomes</cite>. These mechanistic convergences explain the broad protection seen across models and tissues and motivate rational comparative and combination studies <cite id="968752ec-3">Natural phenolic antioxidants such as rosmarinic acid and carvacrol can counteract aluminum-induced oxidative stress and mitochondrial radical overproduction</cite>.

2) Need for comparative studies of different natural compounds
Evidence to date often relies on specific extracts or single compounds, which can confound conclusions due to variable phytochemical composition and preparation. Comparative frameworks should standardize exposure conditions, extraction solvents, and dosing by active phytochemical content to enable fair comparisons across classes (flavanols, polyphenols, alkaloids, essential oils, amino acids/chelators, and whole-plant preparations) <cite id="5585b703-0">Flavonoids and polyphenols in Tamarindus indica fractions show protective potentials tied to specific secondary metabolites (flavonoids, polyphenols, cis-9-hexadecenal), supporting targeted comparative analyses of compound classes</cite> <cite id="968752ec-2">Moringa leaves contain vitamins C, E, A and key polyphenols (chlorogenic acid, quercetin, gallic acid; flavonols isoquercetin, rutin) with documented radical scavenging and protective efficacy in aluminum chloride–treated rats</cite>. Head-to-head designs should measure mechanistic endpoints relevant to aluminum toxicity—lipid peroxidation, GSH depletion, caspase activation, microglial activation, Aβ/tau pathology, cholinesterase inhibition, and hepatic/renal biomarkers—across in vitro, in vivo, and ex vivo human tissue models to reduce translation gaps <cite id="968752ec-3">Aluminum elevates ROS and mitochondrial stress; rosmarinic acid/carvacrol phenolics address these mechanistic axes in counteraction</cite>. Finally, time-course and dose-ranging comparisons should capture differences in metal-chelation kinetics versus antioxidant/anti-inflammatory potency, and include safety/side-effect profiles and interactions (iron co-toxicity modulation) to inform patient-specific regimens <cite id="968752ec-0">Curcumin nanoforms increase absorption >40-fold and cross the BBB; several natural compounds also reduce iron toxicity by preventing absorption and tissue damage, underscoring interaction and safety considerations</cite>.

3) Role of nanotechnology and delivery systems
A central bottleneck for clinical translation is low bioavailability of key natural compounds. Nanocarriers (polymeric nanoparticles, nanoemulsions, liposomes, phytosomes, solid-lipid and nanostructured lipid carriers) can boost solubility, stability, absorption, and brain targeting for hydrophobic phenolics like curcumin and EGCG, enabling higher brain concentrations to tackle neurotoxicity and microglial inflammation <cite id="71ef0cf2-0">Polymeric nanoparticles and nanoemulsions enhance solubility, stability, and targeted delivery of low-bioavailable phytonutrients such as curcumin and EGCG</cite> <cite id="71ef0cf2-1">Advanced curcumin delivery platforms (micelles, polymeric nanoparticles, liposomes, nanocrystals, phytosomes, hydrogels) overcome poor solubility/stability/bioavailability, but require careful assessment for off-targets and carrier toxicity</cite> <cite id="71ef0cf2-2">Zein nanoparticles can incorporate high curcumin levels and better limit oxidation than oil-in-water nanoemulsions; nanoemulsions excel in GI solubilization and mixed micelle formation, with combined systems improving bioaccessibility and stability</cite> <cite id="71ef0cf2-3">Nanoemulsions of essential oils (e.g., lemongrass, rosemary, lemon, lavender, marigold, patchouli) show superior performance; curcumin nanoemulsions enhance dispersibility, stability, release, and bioavailability, enabling therapeutic applications</cite> <cite id="71ef0cf2-4">Nanocarriers (liposomes, nanoemulsions, polymeric micelles, dendrimers, polymeric nanoparticles, solid-lipid and nanostructured lipid carriers) enhance curcumin solubility, bioavailability, and efficacy; regulatory approval and safety remain active considerations</cite>. In aluminum contexts, nanoformulated curcumin has already demonstrated >40-fold absorption increases and CNS availability in pharmacological reviews, paralleling mechanistic benefits on mitochondria and amyloid pathways; analogous nano-delivery should be explored for hesperidin, quercetin, resveratrol, carnosine, and essential oils to correct dose-limited exposure and improve BBB/BCIS crossing <cite id="968752ec-0">Nanosized curcumin increases absorption over 40-fold, biodistributes widely, and crosses the BBB; other flavonoids (naringin, hesperidin) and carnosine attenuate mitochondrial damage and neuroinflammation in aluminum-exposed models</cite>. For chelation-centric approaches, the broader pharmaceutical literature on hydroxypyridinone-based nano-chelators illustrates how high-affinity aluminum complexes can be delivered systemically and may support clinical testing when adapted to natural chelators like phytate and polyphenolic ligands <cite id="5585b703-3">3-Hydroxy-4-pyridinones (hydroxypyridinones) are high-affinity iron chelators that also form highly stable aluminum complexes and may be appropriate for clinical testing to reduce aluminum body burden</cite>. To avoid safety pitfalls, development should enforce pharmaceutical-grade excipients, rigorous impurity control, and preclinical assessments of carrier-induced oxidative stress and metal-redox interactions <cite id="71ef0cf2-1">A compounded curcumin emulsion with non-pharmaceutical PEG-40 castor oil was implicated in contamination and fatalities; nanoformulations must be assessed for off-targets, dose ceilings, and carrier-associated toxicity</cite>.

4) Combining natural products with lifestyle interventions
Diet, microbiome health, and physical activity can amplify or constrain the efficacy of natural compounds against aluminum toxicity. Probiotics can reduce tissue aluminum burden and mitigate multi-organ damage, suggesting synbiotic strategies where fermented polyphenol-rich foods or phytate-rich fibers feed beneficial taxa while lowering aluminum bioavailability and tissue accumulation <cite id="968752ec-0">The probiotic Lactobacillus plantarum CCFM639 significantly protected multiple organs (including brain) and lowered aluminum levels in aluminum-exposed models</cite>. Polyphenol-rich diets (Moringa leaves; rosmarinic/carvacrol phenolics) supply endogenous antioxidants and metal-chelating ligands that counter ROS and metal-protein interactions, and their bioavailability is improved by co-consumption with lipids or encapsulation, pointing to food-integrated delivery via nanoemulsions <cite id="968752ec-2">Moringa leaves act as antioxidant and chelation-like sources of vitamins and polyphenols with protective efficacy in aluminum chloride–treated rats</cite> <cite id="968752ec-3">Dietary phenolics (rosmarinic acid, carvacrol) can counteract aluminum-induced oxidative and mitochondrial stress</cite> <cite id="71ef0cf2-3">Nanoemulsions of essential oils and phenolic-rich extracts enhance dispersibility and bioavailability, supporting diet–delivery integration</cite>. Exercise and physical activity generally reduce oxidative stress, improve mitochondrial quality control, and can potentiate flavonoid actions; while direct aluminum–exercise interaction data are limited in humans, mechanistic literature on heavy metals shows that antioxidant-rich diets, taurine, and flavonoids synergize through shared pathways (ROS scavenging, metal-chelation, and detoxification induction), suggesting combined lifestyle-nutrient protocols for risk-reduction and mitigation <cite id="5585b703-1">Natural antioxidants (flavonoids, carotenoids, vitamin C/E, taurine, gallic acid, curcumin) increase methylation capacity and ROS scavenging, induce phase II detoxification and CYP enzymes, with flavonoids acting as metal chelators and improving hematological and hepatic/renal profiles in toxicant models</cite>. Translationally, stacking strategies should be tested in controlled crossover trials: pairing standardized polyphenol extracts (EGCG, quercetin, resveratrol, anthocyanins) with timed-release phytate fibers, fermented polyphenol foods, and moderate exercise, and monitoring biomarkers (urinary aluminum, 8-OHdG, lipofuscin, neuroinflammatory cytokines) over months to capture slow-changes dynamics <cite id="968752ec-0">Several natural compounds have few/no side effects and can reduce co-toxic metals (e.g., iron) while improving mitochondrial function; standardized nanoforms may enhance safety and efficacy for stacking with lifestyle changes</cite>.

5) Bridging preclinical and clinical studies
Human-relevant translation requires aligning exposures, biomarkers, and risk populations. Aluminum exposure biomarkers (serum/urinary aluminum; brain imaging proxies; CSF metal/protein markers) should be integrated with mechanistic readouts (lipid peroxidation, GSH/GPx activity, ferritin/hepcidin axes, microglial activation, synaptic proteins) to define endpoints that predict clinical benefit in domains like neurocognitive decline, fatigue, and musculoskeletal pain <cite id="968752ec-1">Aluminum exposure elevates organ burdens with oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction, motivating antioxidant/chelation strategies and clinically actionable biomarkers</cite>. Clinical development can leverage precedents from metal chelation: desferrioxamine improved moderate-to-late Alzheimer’s patients when used with the first-generation antioxidant and aluminum/iron chelator, and second-generation selective aluminum chelators (feralex-G) show higher specificity and efficacy in preliminary work—proof-of-concept that chelation plus redox modulation can change disease trajectories, albeit with toxicity and route-of-administration constraints <cite id="5585b703-2">Desferrioxamine, an antioxidant and trivalent iron/aluminum chelator, was the most effective clinical treatment yet for moderate-to-late Alzheimer’s disease; second-generation aluminum chelators like Feralex-G show higher specificity and efficacy in preliminary studies</cite> <cite id="5585b703-3">Deferoxamine is expensive, toxic, non-selective, and non-oral; hydroxypyridinones have high affinity for ferric iron and high stability with aluminum and may be suitable for clinical testing</cite>. Natural-product programs should start with open-label pilot trials in high-exposure groups (hemodialysis patients, workers in aluminum production, cookware users) where aluminum burden is elevated and clinical outcomes are measurable, then escalate to Alzheimer’s spectrum disorders with biomarker-confirmed brain aluminum/proteinopathy signatures. Dosing should be informed by pharmacokinetic modeling and microdose-tox studies of nanoformulated extracts, with pharmacovigilance for interactions (iron/lead), and quality assurance for consistent phytochemical profiles and excipient purity <cite id="71ef0cf2-1">Curcumin nanoformulation development underscores the need to assess off-targets, dose ceilings, and carrier-associated toxicity; pharmaceutical-grade manufacturing and quality control are essential</cite> <cite id="968752ec-0">Nanocurcumin shows >40-fold absorption increase and BBB crossing; several natural compounds are generally safe with few side effects, but dosing and long-term safety still require structured evaluation</cite>.

Practical design elements for future studies
- Comparative platforms: standardized aluminum exposure (i.p./gavage AlCl3 or aluminum-containing diet), co-treatment windows (preventive vs. therapeutic), and orthogonal readouts (ROS, mitochondrial respiration, caspase, cytokines, AChE, hepatic/renal enzymes) to compare flavonoids, polyphenols, alkaloids, essential oils, amino-acid chelators, and whole-plant extracts across mechanistic strata <cite id="5585b703-0">Flavonoids/polyphenols provide antioxidant and chelation-like protection; specific metabolites correlate with improved developmental outcomes in aluminum-exposed prenatal rat cortex</cite>.
- Nano-enabled arms: curcumin/EGCG/anthocyanin and carnosine nanoforms, phytate-loaded nanoparticles, essential oil nanoemulsions, with bioavailability and BBB/P-gp permeation studies and stability under GI conditions <cite id="71ef0cf2-0">Nanoparticles and nanoemulsions enhance solubility, stability, and targeted delivery of low-bioavailable phytonutrients</cite> <cite id="71ef0cf2-2">Comparative nano-delivery systems (zein nanoparticles vs. nanoemulsions vs. phospholipid nanoparticles) show complementary strengths in encapsulation, stability, and release</cite>.
- Lifestyle combinations: randomized crossovers combining standardized polyphenol extracts with phytate-rich fiber, fermented polyphenol foods, and moderate aerobic exercise, measuring short-term oxidative stress and longer-term cognitive/motor outcomes and aluminum biomarkers <cite id="5585b703-1">Dietary flavonoids and antioxidants induce detoxification and act as metal chelators, improving hematological and hepatic/renal profiles in toxicant models</cite> <cite id="968752ec-0">Probiotics can lower aluminum levels and protect multiple organs; natural compounds generally have favorable safety profiles</cite>.
- Translational ladders: start with dialysis-associated aluminum overload cohorts, then community exposures with elevated hair/serum aluminum, and finally AD cohorts with CSF/amyloid/tau/proton MR signatures; incorporate mechanistic imaging (fMRI/DTI) and wearable stress markers to capture synaptic and mitochondrial benefits predicted by preclinical models <cite id="5585b703-2">Clinical studies of next-generation aluminum chelators combined with other strategies are needed to address aluminum neurotoxicity mechanisms</cite>.
- Safety and regulation: adopt good nanopharmaceutical practices—define critical quality attributes, microbial and residual solvent limits, and carry out tox studies for carriers; pre-specify stopping rules for metal-redox signal changes and monitor interactions with iron/lead therapies <cite id="71ef0cf2-1">Contaminated emulsions led to adverse events; nanoformulations must be rigorously evaluated for off-targets and carrier toxicity</cite>.

Summary
Natural compounds offer multi-actor, multi-target strategies to combat aluminum toxicity—chelating, scavenging, anti-inflammatory, and mitochondrial-supportive—demonstrated across cells, animals, and tissues, with translational precedents from metal chelation and supportive clinical signals in Alzheimer’s disease <cite id="968752ec-0">Natural products can chelate or neutralize aluminum, cross the BBB in nanoform, and improve mitochondrial and inflammatory endpoints with generally favorable safety</cite> <cite id="968752ec-1">Exposure routes and organ burdens justify antioxidant and chelation approaches</cite> <cite id="5585b703-2">Desferrioxamine-based therapy improved moderate-to-late AD outcomes; next-generation aluminum chelators warrant focused study</cite>. To accelerate clinical impact, the field should prioritize standardized, mechanistically grounded comparative studies; nano-enabled delivery tailored to absorption and barrier penetration; clinically actionable lifestyle stacking; and phased clinical translation with robust biomarkers and quality systems—leveraging the convergence of diet, microbiome, and nanomedicine to reduce aluminum’s systemic and neurotoxic burden <cite id="71ef0cf2-0">Nanocarriers can convert low-bioavailable phytonutrients into effective therapeutics</cite> <cite id="5585b703-3">Hydroxypyridinone-based aluminum chelation exemplifies candidate platforms for clinical testing and cross-pollination with natural ligands</cite>.

There are currently no treatments for AD that effectively prevent or cure AD's insidious onset or propagation. Snippet: ALUMINUM salts are known to exhibit toxicity to a variety of organs including the nervous system. Although aluminum certainly forms the basis of dialysis dementia, the role of this nonessential element in the etiology of Alzheimer's disease is more controversial ( 4 ). It has been claimed that chelation of aluminum with deferoxamine may ameliorate this disease (24). The mechanistic basis of any aluminum neurotoxicity is also not obvious; however, several reports suggest that a key feature may be an interaction with iron leading to excessive formation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) (6,14,28). This concept finds further support from evidence that amyloid deposits and neurofibrillary tangles found in cortical tissues in Alzheimer's disease have been reported to contain aluminum (12,34), although not all studies confirm this. Amyloid deposits appear able to promote ROS formation (16,32). There is other evidence that this disease involves deleterious free radical-induced events (8,29). 

These issues, together with problems associated with excess levels of aluminum following renal impairment, have driven a search for appropriate chelators to facilitate aluminum excretion. Deferoxamine, the most widely used metal chelator, is rather expensive, toxic, nonselcctive, and cannot be orally administered. A new class of chelators, the 3-hydroxy-4-pyridinones, have been developed initially as potential iron chelators in view of their high affinity for ferric iron (10,17,18). These agents can also form aluminum complexes of high stability (9), and may be appropriate for clinical testing as possible drugs for reducing the body burden of this element (2,36). 

In view of both the potentiation of iron-effected ROS gen-eration by aluminum salts and the potential for certain metal chelators to enhance the pro-oxidant properties of metals ( 1 ,35), we have examined the ROS-promoting capacity of two hydroxypyridinones in an isolated cerebral particulate fraction.

The primary action is the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which inactivate natural antioxidants, such as superoxide dismutase, and glutathione, and increase lipid peroxidation, oxidation of proteins, and damage DNA [12]. The final result of this oxidative condition is the stimulation of microglia and astrocytes and the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, including tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha) and interleukin-6 (IL-6) [13]. Title: Natural Compounds Rosmarinic Acid and Carvacrol Counteract Aluminium-Induced Oxidative Stress
Snippet: Numerous studies have demonstrated the toxicity of aluminum in various animal models [1]. The most important concern about aluminum exposure is related to its neurotoxic effects and its possible role in neurodegenerative disorders [6,34]. Most literature data about the low dose Al toxicity is based on the experiments where Al is administered orally. Direct evidence of neurotoxicity due to low doses of Al is controversial, e.g., Shoji et al. reported that 0.97-9.7 mg/kg/day Al per os for 60 days did not induce statistically significant behavioral changes in C57BL/6J mice [35], whereas Martinez et al. found that 8.3 mg/kg/day Al per os for 60 days promoted the development of mechanical allodynia, catalepsy, increased inflammation in the sciatic nerve, and systemic oxidative stress, and was able to be retained in the sciatic nerve [36]. 

The toxicity of soluble Al forms depends upon the delivered dose of Al 3+ to target tissues. Elevated Al 3+ concentrations lead to Al 3+ -induced formation of oxygen radicals causing lipid peroxidation, which results in cell membrane damage and oxidative stress [3][4][5][6][7]. Accumulating evidence obtained from in vitro, in vivo, and clinical studies supports the free radical scavenging properties of natural phenolic antioxidants [24]. In this study, we proposed that natural herbal phenolic compounds with strong antioxidant activity, such as rosmarinic acid [24] and carvacrol [29], could help to counteract the toxicity of Al. 

Endogenous ROS are mainly produced in the mitochondrial inner membrane during the process of oxidative phosphorylation. The uncontrolled formation of free radicals and activated oxygen species is prevented by intracellular antioxidant systems [37]. Intracellular antioxidants include low molecular weight scavengers of oxidizing species (such as GSH), and enzymes that degrade superoxide and hydroperoxides [37,38].

Snippet: A cautionary case is the FDA's (2017) investigation of a compounded curcumin emulsion product containing non-pharmaceutical grade PEG-40 castor oil. This product was implicated in hypersensitivity, contamination (diethylene glycol), and fatal adverse events (FDA, 2017). Thus, while curcumin has a favorable safety record, The various advanced drug delivery systems designed to enhance the bioavailability and therapeutic efficacy of curcumin. Curcumin, a hydrophobic compound derived from Curcuma longa, faces challenges in clinical applications due to its poor solubility, stability, and bioavailability. To overcome these limitations, multiple drug delivery platforms have been developed. The delivery systems illustrated include micelles, nanoparticles, and solid-lipid nanoparticles (NPs), which improve curcumin's solubility and stability. Liposomes and lipid-based nanoparticles (lipid NPs) enhance the encapsulation and controlled release of curcumin. Polymeric nanoparticles (NPs) offer targeted delivery capabilities, while nanocrystals increase curcumin's dissolution rate. Emulsions serve as simple and effective carriers for curcumin's solubilization. Additionally, innovative systems such as phytosomes, curcumin hydrogels, and carbon nanotubes are highlighted. Phytosomes are complexes that improve curcumin's absorption by interacting with phospholipids, while curcumin hydrogels provide sustained release and localized delivery. Carbon nanotubes, with their unique structural properties, enable efficient drug loading and transport.

Title: Zein-based nano-delivery systems for encapsulation and protection of hydrophobic bioactives: A review
Snippet: Nano-sized delivery systems such as nanoparticles, nanofibers, nanomicelles, nanogels and nanoemulsions have been proved to possess several protective functional advantages for bioactives. Comparatively, zein-based nanoparticles have higher barrier properties than oil-in-water nanoemulsion in limiting peroxyl radical-induced oxidation processes of encapsulated curcumin (99). However, these two encapsulation systems were ineffectiveness in limiting oxygen permeation. In a comparative study of improving curcumin bioavailability by three potential delivery systems (ZNPs, nanoemulsions, and phospholipid nanoparticles), ZNPs were able to incorporate the highest level of curcumin per unit mass of particles. Nevertheless, nanoemulsions appeared to be the most effective at promoting both the chemical stability and solubilization of curcumin at an equal initial curcumin level, under simulated gastrointestinal conditions (100). Chuacharoen and Sabliov (101) also synthesized nanoemulsions and nanoparticles with entrapped curcumin at the same level of surfactant concentration. Compared with nanoemulsions, zein-based nanoparticles were found to be the better carriers based on their storage stability and sustained release profile. 

To fully utilize the advantages of different systems, is it possible to achieve better encapsulation and delivery of hydrophobic bioactives if two or more systems are combined? 

The advantages and disadvantages of different nano-sized delivery systems are summarized in Table 2. Reportedly, mixing curcumin-loaded ZNPs with lipid nanoparticles can increase the bioaccessibility and chemical stability of lipophilic bioactive agents (100). ZNPs can be designed to protect the curcumin from chemical degradation, whereas another type of nanoparticles (like lipid nanoparticles) can be designed to rapidly digest within the gastrointestinal tract and form mixed micelles that can solubilize and transport the hydrophobic curcumin.

Title: Advances in Nanocarrier Systems for Overcoming Formulation Challenges of Curcumin: Current Insights
Snippet: Curcumin, an organic phenolic molecule that is extracted from the rhizomes of Curcuma longa Linn, has undergone extensive evaluation for its diverse biological activities in both animals and humans. Despite its favorable characteristics, curcumin encounters various formulation challenges and stability issues that can be effectively addressed through the application of nanotechnology. Nano-based techniques specifically focused on enhancing solubility, bioavailability, and therapeutic efficacy while mitigating toxicity, have been explored for curcumin. This review systematically presents information on the improvement of curcumin’s beneficial properties when incorporated, either individually or in conjunction with other drugs, into diverse nanosystems such as liposomes, nanoemulsions, polymeric micelles, dendrimers, polymeric nanoparticles, solid-lipid nanoparticles, and nanostructured lipid carriers. Additionally, the review examines ongoing clinical trials and recently granted patents, offering a thorough overview of the dynamic landscape in curcumin delivery. Researchers are currently exploring nanocarriers with crucial features such as surface modification, substantial loading capacity, biodegradability, compatibility, and autonomous targeting specificity and selectivity. Nevertheless, the utilization of nanocarriers for curcumin delivery is still in its initial phases, with regulatory approval pending and persistent safety concerns surrounding their use.
